courses.title: Therapeutic Exercise and Electrotherapy
courses.description: Principles of exercise prescription, strength, endurance, flexibility and balance training, and electrophysical agents in physiotherapy.

topics.title: Principles of Exercise Prescription
topics.summary: FITT principle, overload, specificity, progression and exercise safety.

material.heading: Training principles
material.body: Exercise prescription follows the FITT principle: Frequency, Intensity, Time (duration) and Type — often extended to FITT-VP (Volume, Progression). Key principles: overload (the body must be stressed beyond its usual level to adapt), specificity (adaptations are specific to the type of training — SAID: specific adaptation to imposed demands), progression (gradual increase in load), reversibility ('use it or lose it' — detraining), and individuality. Intensity for aerobic exercise may be set by heart rate reserve (Karvonen method: target HR = [(HRmax − HRrest) × intensity] + HRrest; HRmax ≈ 220 − age), percentage of VO2max, or the Borg rating of perceived exertion (RPE 6–20 scale; about 12–14 = moderate).

material.heading: Safety
material.body: Pre-exercise screening identifies cardiovascular, metabolic and musculoskeletal risks. Sessions include a warm-up (5–10 minutes) and cool-down. Stop exercise for chest pain, severe breathlessness, dizziness, palpitations, pallor or confusion. Contraindications include unstable angina, uncontrolled hypertension (e.g. resting BP > 180/110 mmHg), acute febrile illness, uncontrolled arrhythmias and acute deep vein thrombosis. People with diabetes should check glucose (risk of hypoglycaemia with insulin) and foot care.
keyPoints: Stop for chest pain, dizziness, severe breathlessness

topics.title: Strength, Endurance and Flexibility Training
topics.summary: Resistance training variables, aerobic endurance, stretching methods and their effects.

material.heading: Strength and endurance
material.body: Resistance training variables: load (often as a percentage of one-repetition maximum, 1RM), repetitions, sets, rest and speed. For strength: roughly 60–80% of 1RM for 8–12 repetitions (general guidance), 2–3 sets; for muscular endurance: lighter loads with more repetitions (15–20+). Progressive resistance exercise (DeLorme's method) increases load as strength improves. Open kinetic chain exercises move the distal segment freely (e.g. seated knee extension); closed kinetic chain exercises fix the distal segment (e.g. squats), promoting co-contraction and function. Aerobic training (e.g. 150 minutes/week of moderate activity per WHO guidance) improves VO2max, stroke volume, capillarisation and mitochondrial density, and lowers resting heart rate and blood pressure.

material.heading: Flexibility
material.body: Flexibility is the range of motion available at a joint. Stretching methods: static stretching (holding a stretch for about 15–30 seconds, repeated), dynamic stretching (controlled movement through range — suitable for warm-up), ballistic stretching (bouncing — higher injury risk), and proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF) techniques such as contract–relax and hold–relax, which use autogenic inhibition (via Golgi tendon organs) and reciprocal inhibition to gain range. Passive range-of-motion exercises maintain joint mobility in patients who cannot move (e.g. unconscious or paralysed patients) and prevent contractures.

topics.title: Electrical Stimulation: TENS and NMES
topics.summary: Current types, pain modulation with TENS, neuromuscular stimulation, and safety.

material.heading: Currents and TENS
material.body: Therapeutic currents: direct (monophasic, continuous — iontophoresis), alternating/biphasic pulsed currents (most TENS and NMES), and interferential current (two medium-frequency currents, e.g. 4,000 Hz and 4,100 Hz, interfering to give a low-frequency beat, 100 Hz, deep in tissues). TENS parameters: conventional (high frequency 80–150 Hz, short pulse, low intensity, comfortable tingling) activates Aβ fibres to 'close the gate'; acupuncture-like TENS (low frequency 2–4 Hz, higher intensity, visible muscle twitch) releases endogenous opioids; burst mode combines both. TENS is useful in labour pain, postoperative pain and chronic musculoskeletal pain.
keyPoints: Interferential: beat frequency deep in tissues

material.heading: NMES and safety
material.body: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation produces muscle contraction to strengthen weak muscles (e.g. quadriceps after knee surgery), re-educate muscles and reduce disuse atrophy; functional electrical stimulation (FES) assists function, e.g. dorsiflexion for foot drop after stroke. Denervated muscle needs long-duration pulses (galvanic/interrupted direct current). Contraindications to electrotherapy include demand pacemakers and implanted electrical devices (especially over the thorax), over the pregnant uterus, over the carotid sinus, over areas of malignancy or active bleeding, broken skin (relative), impaired sensation (relative) and in patients unable to communicate. Test skin sensation before application.
keyPoints: Avoid pacemakers, pregnant uterus, carotid sinus, malignancy

topics.title: Heat, Cold, Ultrasound and Other Electrophysical Agents
topics.summary: Superficial and deep heating, cryotherapy, therapeutic ultrasound, shortwave diathermy and laser.

material.heading: Thermal agents
material.body: Superficial heating (hot packs, paraffin wax — useful for hand arthritis, infrared lamps) penetrates about 1–2 cm, increasing blood flow, tissue extensibility and pain relief. Deep heating: shortwave diathermy (27.12 MHz electromagnetic energy — contraindicated with metal implants, pacemakers, pregnancy) and continuous therapeutic ultrasound. Cryotherapy (ice packs, ice massage, cold sprays) reduces pain, swelling, metabolic rate and muscle spasm; use for 10–20 minutes with a barrier. Hunting response: alternating vasoconstriction and vasodilation with prolonged cold. Contraindications to cold include Raynaud's phenomenon, cold urticaria, cryoglobulinaemia and impaired circulation.

material.heading: Ultrasound and laser
material.body: Therapeutic ultrasound uses frequencies of 1 MHz (deeper, up to ~5 cm) or 3 MHz (superficial, 1–2 cm); a coupling medium (gel) is essential because ultrasound does not travel through air. Continuous mode produces thermal effects; pulsed mode (e.g. 20% duty cycle) produces non-thermal effects (cavitation, acoustic streaming) that may aid tissue healing. The effective radiating area and beam non-uniformity ratio (BNR — lower is safer) describe the transducer; keep the head moving to avoid hot spots. Low-level laser therapy (photobiomodulation) is used for wound healing and pain; protective goggles are required. Hydrotherapy uses warm water's buoyancy and support for exercise.
keyPoints: Keep transducer moving; low BNR safer

topics.title: Exercise for Special Populations
topics.summary: Exercise in older adults, pregnancy, children, chronic diseases and after cardiac events.

material.heading: Older adults and pregnancy
material.body: Older adults benefit from aerobic, strengthening, balance and flexibility training to prevent falls, sarcopenia and osteoporosis; start low, progress slowly, and include functional tasks (sit-to-stand, stair climbing). Weight-bearing and resistance exercise improve bone density. In uncomplicated pregnancy, moderate exercise (about 150 minutes/week) is safe and beneficial — reducing gestational diabetes, excess weight gain and back pain; avoid lying flat on the back for prolonged periods after the first trimester (supine hypotension from aortocaval compression), contact sports, scuba diving, and exercise in heat. Pelvic floor muscle training prevents and treats urinary incontinence. Warning signs to stop: vaginal bleeding, leakage of amniotic fluid, regular painful contractions, chest pain, dizziness, calf pain or swelling.
keyPoints: Older adults: balance and strength to prevent falls
Pregnancy: avoid prolonged supine after first trimester

material.heading: Chronic diseases
material.body: Cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery progresses through phases: inpatient mobilisation (phase I), early post-discharge (phase II), supervised outpatient exercise (phase III) and long-term maintenance (phase IV); it reduces mortality and improves quality of life. Pulmonary rehabilitation for COPD combines exercise training, breathing techniques and education, improving exercise tolerance. In diabetes, exercise improves insulin sensitivity; check glucose before exercise and carry a quick sugar source. In hypertension, regular aerobic exercise lowers blood pressure by about 5–8 mmHg. In osteoarthritis, strengthening (quadriceps) and aerobic exercise reduce pain and improve function. People with sickle cell disease should exercise moderately, stay well hydrated and avoid extremes of temperature.
